extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, biogeographers, and general readers of evolutionary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and explanatory principles used to account for the geographic distribution of species (how identical and allied forms occur in distant regions, freshwater and island distributions, and the effects of past climate). Focuses on historical processes (migration, climate change, dispersal mechanisms) rather than classification rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of past climatic changes (Glacial and Pliocene periods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Past alternations of climate (warmer Pliocene periods and later Glacial epoch) caused large-scale southward and northward migrations and re-distributions of plants and animals, explaining present affinities and disjunctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use geological evidence of warmer Pliocene climates and a subsequent Glacial epoch to explain why temperate species once ranged further poleward and later migrated; invoke long duration and (partly) simultaneous cooling to allow extensive migration and subsequent isolation leading to modification. Examples: temperate plants living under the Polar Circle during Pliocene; later migration southwards and isolation producing related but distinct species in Europe and North America.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of circumpolar land enabling interchange
rubrics_metrics.description: A formerly more continuous circumpolar land (under the Polar Circle) permitted free inter-migration, producing uniformity in sub-arctic and northern temperate productions between Old and New Worlds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On a globe, the land from western Europe through Siberia to eastern America formed almost continuous high-latitude connections; this geographical continuity during warmer periods explains close relationships among northern genera across continents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of glacial belts and longitudinal belts of cooler climate
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if glaciation was not strictly simultaneous everywhere, contemporaneous cooler belts (longitudinally) could account for wide migrations and distributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that the cold may have come earlier or ceased earlier in places, but the long duration and broad belts of lower temperature suffice to permit migrations across large regions (e.g., both sides of North America, equatorial Cordillera, southern extremities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Southern migration plus competition produces greater modification
rubrics_metrics.description: As temperate organisms migrated southwards and mixed with native inhabitants of new regions, competition and differing conditions favoured more extensive modification (speciation) than in isolated alpine or arctic refugia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When migrants mingled with native floras/faunas, they had to compete and often were modified more extensively; conversely, isolated alpine/arctic productions remained less modified. This explains why temperate regions of Old and New Worlds have many allied but distinct species rather than identical ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of similar mountain and temperate floras by migration and climate analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: High mountains in intertropical regions and temperate lowlands can host closely related or identical forms to temperate regions because cooler conditions or past climatic stages allowed temperate species to occupy these heights or latitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples: mountain-summit floras of Java, Himalaya, Brazil, Abyssinia, and Australia exhibiting European genera or northern temperate forms; treat mountains as 'islands' preserving former inhabitants driven up by climatic change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fresh-water dispersal capacities and mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Many freshwater organisms have unexpectedly wide ranges because they possess traits (or are subject to events) that enable short but frequent migrations between ponds/streams and occasional long-distance transport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider mechanisms Darwin documents: change in river levels causing rivers to inosculate; accidental transport of live fish by whirlwinds; ova and just-hatched molluscs clinging to bird feet and surviving 12–20 hours to be carried hundreds of miles; mud adhering to birds carrying large numbers of seeds (Darwin's mud experiment: 537 plants from a teaspoonful); water-birds and herons transporting seeds/eggs in pellets or excrement. Also consider marine-to-freshwater shifts (salt-water fish becoming acclimated), and the lower rates of change in 'low' organisms giving more time for dispersal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dispersal by exceptional agents (icebergs, floating islands, driftwood)
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasional extraordinary means—icebergs, sunken or temporary islands, floating timber—can transport organisms across oceans and explain widely separated identical or closely allied species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply especially to southern hemisphere cases (e.g., identical species at Kerguelen, New Zealand, Fuegia). Lyell's suggestion of icebergs and Darwin's hypothesis of halting places (now sunken islands) are cited as plausible mechanisms for rare long-distance dispersal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patterns of oceanic-island biotas: species-poor but highly endemic
rubrics_metrics.description: Oceanic islands tend to have fewer species than equivalent continental areas but a high proportion of endemics; the composition reflects which groups can reach the island and whether they arrived as established assemblages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use colonisation from the nearest source plus subsequent modification to explain high endemism. Compare examples: New Zealand (few flowering plants but many endemics), Galapagos (many endemic land-birds but few endemic marine birds), Bermuda and Madeira (stocked recurrently by continental migrants and thus fewer endemics in some groups).

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of ease of arrival and pre-adaptation in determining which taxa colonize islands
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxa that arrive frequently and in groups already adapted to each other (e.g., many continental birds) tend not to become endemic or modified, whereas taxa arriving infrequently or singly are more likely to radiate and become peculiar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example contrasts: Bermuda and Madeira receive many continental birds during migration and therefore have no endemic land birds; Galapagos receives land-birds less readily so nearly all land-birds are peculiar. Land-shells vs. sea-shells on Madeira: sea-shells disperse more readily and are not endemic; land-shells are often endemic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anthropogenic introduction and competition accelerate native extinction/naturalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduced (naturalised) species can outcompete and in some cases nearly exterminate native island species; such processes mirror natural colonisation dynamics and affect contemporary island faunas/floras.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe real cases: Ascension originally had very few flowering plants but many have become naturalised by human agency; St. Helena shows near-extermination of natives by naturalised species. Use as caution when inferring original island biotas.
